d: Before: the chapter on preliminaries supplies the two tools used here, the matrix point of view (eigenvalues, powers of a matrix) and linear difference equations (the random-walk equation, particular plus homogeneous solution).
This chapter: Markov chains in discrete time on a finite state space. One matrix $P$ describes everything, and the chapter is about what $P^n$ does for large $n$.
After: the same questions for countably many states (where a chain can escape to infinity), then continuous time.
An invariant probability vector is a row vector $\bar\pi \ge 0$ with $\sum_j\pi(j) = 1$ and $\bar\pi P = \bar\pi$. The chapter asks:
1. Existence: is there such a $\bar\pi$? 2. Uniqueness: only one? 3. Convergence: does $\phi P^n \to \bar\pi$ for every initial distribution $\phi$, i.e. do the rows of $P^n$ all approach $\bar\pi$?
Answer: yes to all three when the chain is irreducible and aperiodic. Reducibility breaks uniqueness, periodicity breaks convergence, and these are the only two obstacles.

Example A, the phone chain: state 0 = free, 1 = busy, $P = \begin{pmatrix}3/4&1/4\\1/6&5/6\end{pmatrix}$ ($p = \tfrac14$, $q = \tfrac16$). Everything can be computed by hand: $\bar\pi = (\tfrac25, \tfrac35)$, second eigenvalue $\tfrac{7}{12}$, mean return time to 0 equal to $\tfrac52$.

Example B, the random walk on $\{0, 1, 2, 3, 4\}$ in two versions. Reflecting ($p(0, 1) = p(4, 3) = 1$): irreducible with period 2, $\bar\pi = (\tfrac18, \tfrac14, \tfrac14, \tfrac14, \tfrac18)$. Absorbing ($p(0, 0) = p(4, 4) = 1$): reducible, states 1, 2, 3 transient.
A third chain, the queue with one hold slot, is used whenever a 3 by 3 example is needed.
$p(i, j)$: one-step transition probability; $P$: the matrix of the $p(i, j)$; $p_n(i, j) = (P^n)_{ij}$: $n$-step probability.
$\phi$: initial distribution (row vector); $\bar\pi$: invariant distribution (row vector); $\bar 1$: the all-ones column.
$d$: period; $T$: return time ($n \ge 1$); $T_i$: hitting time of $i$ ($n \ge 0$).
$Q$: transient-to-transient block; $S$: transient-to-recurrent block; $M = (I - Q)^{-1}$: fundamental matrix; $\alpha$: absorption probability.
$P^n$ = limit + (second eigenvalue)$^n$ $\times$ fixed matrix. For the two-state chain exactly; in general up to faster-decaying terms.

Second eigenvalue of absolute value below 1: convergence at speed $|\lambda|^n$. Equal to $-1$ (or another root of unity): periodic, no convergence. Equal to 1 again: reducible, limit depends on the start.
$\mathbb{P}\{X_n = i_n \mid X_0 = i_0, \dots, X_{n-1} = i_{n-1}\} = \mathbb{P}\{X_n = i_n \mid X_{n-1} = i_{n-1}\}$: to predict the next state only the present state matters.
Time homogeneity: this probability is the same for every $n$; call it $p(i_{n-1}, i_n)$. The transition matrix $P = (p(i, j))$ is a stochastic matrix: entries in $[0, 1]$, every row sums to 1.
With the initial distribution $\phi$, the probability of a whole path is $\phi(i_0)p(i_0, i_1)\cdots p(i_{n-1}, i_n)$. So $\phi$ and $P$ determine the chain.
1. Two-state phone chain: $P = \begin{pmatrix}1-p&p\\q&1-q\end{pmatrix}$, where $p$ = a call arrives while free, $q$ = the call ends while busy.

2. Queue with one hold slot, states 0, 1, 2 callers: $p(1, 0) = q(1-p)$, $p(1, 2) = p(1-q)$, $p(1, 1) = pq + (1-p)(1-q)$; with $p = \tfrac14$, $q = \tfrac16$: $$P = \begin{pmatrix}3/4&1/4&0\\1/8&2/3&5/24\\0&1/6&5/6\end{pmatrix}$$
3. Random walk with reflecting boundary on $\{0, \dots, N\}$: interior steps $\pm1$ with probability $\tfrac12$, $p(0, 1) = p(N, N-1) = 1$.
4. Random walk with absorbing boundary: the same interior, $p(0, 0) = p(N, N) = 1$.
5. Simple random walk on a graph: $p(v, w) = 1/d(v)$ for each neighbour $w$ of $v$. Example 3 is the walk on the path $0 - 1 - \dots - N$.

$p_n(i, j) = \mathbb{P}\{X_n = j \mid X_0 = i\}$. Splitting on the state at time $m$ gives Chapman–Kolmogorov, $p_{m+n}(i, j) = \sum_k p_m(i, k)p_n(k, j)$, which is matrix multiplication. Hence $p_n(i, j) = (P^n)_{ij}$.
Example A: $p_2(0, 0) = \tfrac34\cdot\tfrac34 + \tfrac14\cdot\tfrac16 = \tfrac{29}{48}$ and $p_2(0, 1) = \tfrac{19}{48}$.
Row vector = distribution: if $X_0$ has distribution $\phi$, then $X_n$ has distribution $\phi P^n$. Example A: $\mathbb{P}\{X_6 = 1 \mid X_0 = 0\} \approx .576$.
Column vector = function on the states: $(Pf)(i) = \mathbb{E}[f(X_1) \mid X_0 = i]$. In particular $P\bar 1 = \bar 1$: 1 is always an eigenvalue.

Raise $P$ to a high power and the rows become identical: for the phone chain every row tends to $(\tfrac25, \tfrac35)$, for the queue to $(\tfrac{2}{11}, \tfrac{4}{11}, \tfrac{5}{11}) \approx (.182, .364, .455)$.
Identical rows mean that the chain forgets its starting point.

If $\phi P^n \to \bar\pi$, then $\bar\pi = \lim\phi P^{n+1} = (\lim\phi P^n)P = \bar\pi P$. So the candidates for the limit are the left eigenvectors of $P$ with eigenvalue 1, normalised to be probability vectors.

Solving for the queue: column 0 gives $\pi(1) = 2\pi(0)$, column 2 gives $\pi(2) = \tfrac54\pi(1)$, and $\sum\pi = 1$ gives $(\tfrac{2}{11}, \tfrac{4}{11}, \tfrac{5}{11})$. One of the equations $\bar\pi P = \bar\pi$ is always redundant; the normalisation replaces it.
Eigenvalues: 1 (rows sum to 1) and $\lambda = 1 - p - q$ (the trace is $2 - p - q$). Example A: $\lambda = \tfrac{7}{12}$.
Left eigenvector for 1: $\bar\pi = (\tfrac{q}{p+q}, \tfrac{p}{p+q})$; Example A: $(\tfrac25, \tfrac35)$.
$$P^n = \frac{1}{p+q}\begin{pmatrix}q&p\\q&p\end{pmatrix} + \frac{\lambda^n}{p+q}\begin{pmatrix}p&-p\\-q&q\end{pmatrix}$$
Convergence rests on $|\lambda| < 1$ and its speed is $|\lambda|^n$; in Example A four more steps multiply the deviation by $(\tfrac{7}{12})^4 \approx 0.116$.

Why $0 < p, q < 1$ is assumed: $p = q = 1$ gives $\lambda = -1$, the chain flips every step and $P^n$ alternates between $I$ and $P$ (periodicity); $p = q = 0$ gives $P = I$, where every probability vector is invariant (reducibility).
Two facts were used: (1.9) the left eigenvector for 1 can be chosen with nonnegative entries; (1.10) the eigenvalue 1 is simple and all other eigenvalues have absolute value below 1.

Under them, with the Jordan form $P = QDQ^{-1}$, $D = \begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&B\end{pmatrix}$ and $B^n \to 0$: $P^n \to Q\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}Q^{-1}$ = (first column of $Q$)(first row of $Q^{-1}$) $= \bar 1\bar\pi$, the matrix with every row $\bar\pi$.
The book calls the block $M$ here; these notes write $B$ because $M$ and $Q$ get a different meaning in 1.5.
Theorem: if all entries of a stochastic matrix are positive, then 1 is a simple eigenvalue, its left eigenvector can be chosen positive, and all other eigenvalues have absolute value below 1.

All positive is too strict (the queue has zeros), but the queue's $P^2$ is all positive, e.g. entry $(0, 0) = \tfrac{19}{32}$ and entry $(0, 2) = \tfrac{5}{96}$. Apply the theorem to $P^2$ and pass back to $P$: an eigenvalue $\mu$ of $P$ gives $\mu^2$ for $P^2$ with the same eigenvector, so a second eigenvalue of modulus 1 for $P$ would give one for $P^2$.
Fact: if some $P^n$ has all entries positive, then $P$ satisfies (1.9) and (1.10), and every row of $P^m$ converges to the unique $\bar\pi$.
Open question for the next section: which chains have a power with all entries positive?
Reflecting walk on $\{0, \dots, 4\}$: $P^n$ alternates; row 0 is about $(.25, 0, .5, 0, .25)$ for even $n$ and $(0, .5, 0, .5, 0)$ for odd $n$. Reason: every step changes the parity (period 2).
Absorbing walk: $P^n$ converges but the rows differ, row 1 to $(.75, 0, 0, 0, .25)$, row 2 to $(.5, 0, 0, 0, .5)$, row 3 to $(.25, 0, 0, 0, .75)$. Reason: 1, 2, 3 are transient.

Two blocks side by side ($\{1, 2\}$ with $\begin{pmatrix}1/2&1/2\\1/6&5/6\end{pmatrix}$, $\{3, 4, 5\}$ with the queue): rows 1, 2 tend to $(.25, .75, 0, 0, 0)$, rows 3 to 5 to $(0, 0, .182, .364, .455)$. Reason: reducible.
$i \leftrightarrow j$ when $p_m(i, j) > 0$ and $p_n(j, i) > 0$ for some $m, n \ge 0$. It is an equivalence relation; transitivity because $p_{m_1+m_2}(i, k) \ge p_{m_1}(i, j)p_{m_2}(j, k)$.
The classes partition the state space; one class only = irreducible. Reflecting walk: one class. Absorbing walk: $\{0\}$, $\{1, 2, 3\}$, $\{4\}$. Two blocks: $\{1, 2\}$, $\{3, 4, 5\}$.
A transient class is left for good with probability 1; a recurrent class is never left. For a finite chain: recurrent = closed (nothing outside can be reached). There is at least one recurrent class.
Canonical form, recurrent classes first and transient states last: $$P = \begin{pmatrix}\tilde P&0\\S&Q\end{pmatrix},\qquad P^n = \begin{pmatrix}\tilde P^n&0\\S_n&Q^n\end{pmatrix}$$

$\tilde P$ is block diagonal with one stochastic block $P_k$ per recurrent class; $S$ = transient to recurrent, $Q$ = transient to transient. The long-run behaviour on $R_k$ only involves $P_k$; $Q^n$ is the subject of 1.5.

items.t: A wrong sentence in the book
d: “Any matrix satisfying (1.9) and (1.10) is irreducible” is false: $\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1/2&1/2\end{pmatrix}$ has eigenvalues $1, \tfrac12$ and left eigenvector $(1, 0)$, yet state 1 is transient.
Correct: if some $P^n$ is all positive the chain is irreducible; or (1.9), (1.10) plus $\pi(i) > 0$ for all $i$.

For an irreducible chain, $d(i) = \gcd\{n \ge 0 : p_n(i, i) > 0\}$. Reflecting walk: returns to 0 only at even times, $d = 2$. Queue: $p(0, 0) > 0$, $d = 1$. Rule of thumb: a self-loop makes the chain aperiodic.
The set $J_i$ of possible return times is closed under addition, so (number-theory lemma) it contains all large multiples of $d$: $p_{md}(i, i) > 0$ for all large $m$.

All states of an irreducible chain have the same period: with $p_m(i, j) > 0$, $p_n(j, i) > 0$ and $l \in J_j$, both $m + n$ and $m + l + n$ lie in $J_i$, so $d(i)$ divides $l$; hence $d(i)$ divides $d(j)$, and by symmetry they are equal.
Graph walks: the period is 1 or 2 (there and back is a loop of length 2), and it is 2 exactly for bipartite graphs. Path and 4-cycle: 2. 5-cycle: 1.

Irreducible + aperiodic implies some $P^n$ is all positive: $p_n(i, i) > 0$ for $n \ge M(i)$ (aperiodic), $p_{m(i,j)}(i, j) > 0$ (irreducible), so $p_{n+m(i,j)}(i, j) > 0$ for $n \ge M(i)$; take the maximum of $M(i) + m(i, j)$ over the finitely many pairs.
Theorem: for an irreducible aperiodic chain there is a unique invariant $\bar\pi$, $\lim_n\phi P^n = \bar\pi$ for every $\phi$, and every $\pi(i) > 0$.
Dropping a hypothesis: $P = I$ (reducible) loses uniqueness; $P = \begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ (periodic) loses convergence.

Each recurrent class $R_k$ is a chain of its own with invariant distribution $\bar\pi^k$; the eigenvalue 1 has multiplicity $r$ = number of recurrent classes, and every mixture of the $\bar\pi^k$ is invariant.

Limits (each $P_k$ aperiodic): from $i \in R_k$, $p_n(i, j) \to \pi^k(j)$; to a transient $j$, the limit is 0; from a transient $i$ to $j \in R_k$, $p_n(i, j) \to \alpha_k(i)\pi^k(j)$, where $\alpha_k(i)$ is the probability of falling into $R_k$.
Absorbing walk: $\lim p_n(1, 0) = \tfrac34 \cdot 1$. How to compute $\alpha_k(i)$ is in 1.5.

The states split into $d$ groups visited cyclically. There are $d$ eigenvalues of modulus 1 (the roots of $z^d = 1$). $\bar\pi$ exists and is unique, but $\phi P^n$ cycles through $d$ distributions; their average is $\bar\pi$.

Reflecting walk: eigenvalues $1, -1, 0, \pm\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$, $\bar\pi = (\tfrac18, \tfrac14, \tfrac14, \tfrac14, \tfrac18)$. $p_n(0, 0)$ is close to $\tfrac18 + \tfrac18 = \tfrac14$ for even $n$ and $\tfrac18 - \tfrac18 = 0$ for odd $n$; $\pi(0) = \tfrac18$ is the average of two consecutive steps.
Compare with Example A: $P^n = \bar 1\bar\pi + (\tfrac{7}{12})^n(\dots)$ there, $P^n \approx \bar 1\bar\pi + (-1)^n(\dots)$ here; the deviation term flips sign and never decays.
Irreducible, aperiodic: $\bar\pi$ unique; $P^n \to \bar 1\bar\pi$; $\pi(j)$ = limiting probability = fraction of time. Examples: phone, queue.
Irreducible, period $d$: $\bar\pi$ unique; $P^n$ cycles; $\pi(j)$ = fraction of time only. Example: reflecting walk.
Reducible (recurrent classes aperiodic): one $\bar\pi^k$ per recurrent class; $P^n$ converges but rows differ; $\lim p_n(i, j) = \alpha_k(i)\pi^k(j)$. Examples: absorbing walk, two blocks.

$Y(j, n)$ = number of visits to $j$ up to time $n$. $\mathbb{E}[Y(j, n) \mid X_0 = i]/(n+1) = \tfrac{1}{n+1}\sum_{m=0}^n p_m(i, j) \to \pi(j)$, for periodic chains as well (averages over $d$ steps converge).
Start at $i$, $T = \min\{n \ge 1 : X_n = i\}$. Then $\mathbb{E}(T) = 1/\pi(i)$ (book (1.11)).

Heuristic: the gaps between successive returns are independent copies of $T$, so $k$ returns take about $k\,\mathbb{E}(T)$ steps; in $n$ steps there are about $n\pi(i)$ visits; put $n = k\,\mathbb{E}(T)$.
It uses $\mathbb{E}(T) < \infty$ and the restart at a random time; the rigorous proof is one of the exercises (expected visits during one return cycle form an invariant vector).
Use: the mean return time needs no new equations. Conversely an obvious return time gives $\pi(i)$ for free.
From 0: $\mathbb{P}\{T = 1\} = 1 - p$ and $\mathbb{P}\{T \ge n\} = p(1-q)^{n-2}$ for $n \ge 2$.
Tail-sum formula (1.13): $\mathbb{E}(Y) = \sum_{k \ge 1}\mathbb{P}\{Y \ge k\}$ for a nonnegative integer $Y$.
$\mathbb{E}(T) = 1 + \sum_{n \ge 2}p(1-q)^{n-2} = 1 + \tfrac pq = \tfrac{p+q}{q} = 1/\pi(0)$. Example A: $\tfrac52$; from state 1: $\tfrac53$.
Two-state chain with $p = q$: $\bar\pi = (\tfrac12, \tfrac12)$ and $\mathbb{E}(T) = 2$ for every $p$, yet $\operatorname{Var}(T) = 2(1-p)/p$ is $0.22$ for $p = 0.9$ and $18$ for $p = 0.1$.
Reflecting walk: $\pi(0) = \tfrac18$, so the mean return time to 0 is 8. Section 1.5 finds the same number another way ($1 + 7$).

For transient $i, j$: $p_n(j, i) = (Q^n)_{ji}$, because a path between transient states never passes through a recurrent class. $Q$ has row sums at most 1 (the missing mass flows into recurrent classes) and $Q^n \to 0$, so $I - Q$ is invertible.
Fundamental matrix $M = (I - Q)^{-1} = I + Q + Q^2 + \dots$; $M_{ji}$ = expected number of visits to $i$ starting from $j$ (time 0 included).
Row sums of $M$ = expected number of steps before leaving the transient states: $M\bar 1$.
Transient states 1, 2, 3: $$Q = \begin{pmatrix}0&1/2&0\\1/2&0&1/2\\0&1/2&0\end{pmatrix},\quad M = \begin{pmatrix}3/2&1&1/2\\1&2&1\\1/2&1&3/2\end{pmatrix}$$
$M_{13} = \tfrac12$: from 1, half a visit to 3 on average. $M_{11} = \tfrac32$. Row sums $3, 4, 3$: expected steps until absorption.
In an irreducible chain, make the target $i$ absorbing; then all other states are transient and $\mathbb{E}(T_i \mid X_0 = j)$ is the component $j$ of $M\bar 1$.
Reflecting walk, target 0: $M\bar 1 = (7, 12, 15, 16)$, so from 4 to 0 takes 16 steps. Check with Kac: from 0 one step to 1, then 7 steps: $1 + 7 = 8 = 1/\pi(0)$.
Return time $T$ starts counting at $n = 1$ and uses $1/\pi(i)$; hitting time $T_i$ starts at $n = 0$ and uses $M\bar 1$. Link: $\mathbb{E}_i(T) = 1 + \sum_j p(i, j)\mathbb{E}_j(T_i)$.

Treat each recurrent class as one absorbing point. $\alpha(t, r)$ = probability of being absorbed at $r$ from the transient state $t$. First step: $\alpha(t, r) = p(t, r) + \sum_{z\ \text{transient}}p(t, z)\alpha(z, r)$, i.e. $A = S + QA$, so $A = MS$.
Absorbing walk: $MS = \begin{pmatrix}3/4&1/4\\1/2&1/2\\1/4&3/4\end{pmatrix}$ (columns 0 and 4). This is where the limit $(.75, 0, 0, 0, .25)$ of row 1 of $P^n$ comes from.

Capital $j$, win 1 with probability $p$, lose 1 with probability $1 - p$, stop at 0 or $N$. $\alpha(j)$ = probability of reaching $N$ first: $\alpha(j) = (1-p)\alpha(j-1) + p\alpha(j+1)$, $\alpha(0) = 0$, $\alpha(N) = 1$ (book (1.15)).
With $\rho = \tfrac{1-p}{p}$: $\alpha(j) = \dfrac{1 - \rho^j}{1 - \rho^N}$ for $p \ne \tfrac12$ and $\alpha(j) = \tfrac jN$ for $p = \tfrac12$.
$N = 4$: fair game $\tfrac14, \tfrac12, \tfrac34$; $p = \tfrac23$: $\tfrac{8}{15}, \tfrac45, \tfrac{14}{15}$.
$N \to \infty$: for $p \le \tfrac12$ the limit is 0 (ruin is certain); for $p > \tfrac12$ it is $1 - \rho^j > 0$.
Fair game: $G(j) = 1 + \tfrac12G(j-1) + \tfrac12G(j+1)$, $G(0) = G(N) = 0$ (book (1.17)). Particular solution $-j^2$, homogeneous solutions $c_1 + c_2j$, constants $c_1 = 0$, $c_2 = N$.
$G(j) = j(N - j)$ (book (1.18)). $N = 4$: $3, 4, 3$, the row sums of $M$. From the middle: $N^2/4$ rounds, the square scale typical of a random walk.
Absorption probability $f$: $f = 1$ at the target, 0 at other absorbing states, $f(x) = \sum_y p(x, y)f(y)$; matrix form $MS$.
Expected steps $g$: $g = 0$ at absorbing states, $g(x) = 1 + \sum_y p(x, y)g(y)$; matrix form $M\bar 1$.
Expected visits to $i$, $h$: $h = 0$ at absorbing states, $h(x) = I\{x = i\} + \sum_y p(x, y)h(y)$; column $i$ of $M$.
Absorbing walk from 1: $\tfrac34$ (to 0), 3 steps, $\tfrac12$ visit to 3.

Connected graph with $e$ edges: $\pi(v) = d(v)/2e$. Check: $\sum_{v \sim w}\tfrac{d(v)}{2e}\cdot\tfrac{1}{d(v)} = \tfrac{d(w)}{2e}$. Path $0 - \dots - 4$: $(\tfrac18, \tfrac14, \tfrac14, \tfrac14, \tfrac18)$.

$N$ points, steps $\pm1$ with probability $\tfrac12$. $T_k$ = first time $k$ points have been visited. At $T_{k-1}$ the walker is at an end of the visited arc; $r(k) = 1 + \tfrac12[(k - 3) + r(k)]$, so $r(k) = k - 1$ and $\mathbb{E}[T_N] = \tfrac{N(N-1)}{2}$ ($N = 5$: 10).
The last point visited is uniform on $\{1, \dots, N-1\}$.

$N$ balls, a random ball changes colour with probability $\tfrac12$: $p(j, j \pm 1) = \tfrac{N-j}{2N}, \tfrac{j}{2N}$, $p(j, j) = \tfrac12$. Invariant distribution binomial, $\pi(j) = \binom Nj2^{-N}$; return to all green takes $2^N$ steps on average.

$p(j, k) = \binom{2j}{k}\binom{2N-2j}{N-k}/\binom{2N}{N}$; 0 and $N$ absorbing; $\alpha(j) = \tfrac jN$ because the expected fraction of type I is preserved, and a function satisfying the one-step equation and the boundary values is the absorption probability.

Random card to the top: irreducible, aperiodic (self-loop), doubly stochastic, so $\bar\pi$ is uniform on the $n!$ orderings. By Kac the original order of 52 cards returns after $52!$ steps on average.
1.1 newspaper pile: states $0, \dots, 4$, $p(i, 0) = \tfrac13$, $p(i, i+1) = \tfrac23$, $p(4, 0) = 1$. 1.2: $\mathbb{P}\{X_3 = 1\} = \tfrac{109}{216}$.
1.3: $\bar\pi = \tfrac{1}{66}(25, 17, 24)$. 1.4 (same task, another matrix): $\bar\pi = \tfrac{1}{39}(11, 16, 12)$.
1.6: return to state 2 in the chain of 1.3: $\tfrac{66}{17}$. 1.13: newspaper pile, $\bar\pi = \tfrac{1}{211}(81, 54, 36, 24, 16)$, mean $\tfrac{262}{211}$, return to 0 in $\tfrac{211}{81}$.
1.9: period 3, $\bar\pi = (\tfrac13, \tfrac19, \tfrac29, \tfrac{5}{36}, \tfrac{7}{36})$, return time to 1 always 3, $p_{1000}(2, 4) \approx \tfrac{5}{12}$.
1.8 (five-vertex graph): $\pi(A) = \tfrac14$; return to $A$: 4; visits to $B$ from $C$ before $A$: $\tfrac{9}{11}$; reach $A$ before $C$ from $B$: $\tfrac47$; steps from $C$ to $A$: $\tfrac{29}{11}$.
1.19 (four heads in a row): 30 flips.
1.17 complete graph: return $N$, hit $N - 1$, cover $(N-1)\sum_{m=1}^{N-1}\tfrac1m$. 1.18: $52!$ seconds $\approx 2.56 \times 10^{60}$ years.
1.7: the probability of not reaching $j$ in $n$ steps is at most $C\rho^n$, so return times have finite mean. 1.15: rigorous Kac. 1.16: last point on the circle is uniform.
1.20: Perron–Frobenius (largest $\lambda$ with $A\bar v \ge \lambda\bar v$; apply to the transpose for $\bar\pi$). 1.21: a set closed under addition with gcd $d$ contains almost all multiples of $d$.
1.7 and 1.15 are the two foundations that later calculations rely on silently.
1. Model: write the states and $P$; check that every row sums to 1.
2. Draw the graph and classify: communication classes; closed classes are recurrent, the rest transient.
3. Period of each recurrent class: a self-loop gives 1; otherwise the gcd of loop lengths, or check for a bipartite graph.
4. Pick the tool for the question (next item).
5. Cross-check: rows sum to 1; $\sum\pi = 1$; Kac agrees with one-step equations ($8 = 1 + 7$); rows of $MS$ sum to 1.
Probability at step $n$: $\phi P^n$. Example: $.576$.
Long-run fraction of time at $j$ (irreducible, periodic is fine): solve $\bar\pi P = \bar\pi$, $\sum\pi = 1$; graph walk: $d(v)/2e$. Example: queue $(\tfrac{2}{11}, \tfrac{4}{11}, \tfrac{5}{11})$.
$p_n(i, j)$ for large $n$: aperiodic $\pi(j)$; periodic by cyclic group; reducible $\alpha_k(i)\pi^k(j)$. Example: absorbing walk $\tfrac34$.
Mean return time (irreducible): Kac, $1/\pi(i)$. Examples: phone $\tfrac52$, reflecting walk 8.
Mean steps from $j$ to $i \ne j$: make $i$ absorbing, $M\bar 1$, or one-step equations. Example: 16.
Reach $A$ before $B$: make both absorbing, $MS$, or one-step equations. Example: gambler's ruin.
Visits to a state before absorption: the entry of $M$. Example: $M_{13} = \tfrac12$.
The book uses the same $\bar v$ for both. $\bar\pi P$: a distribution (row). $P\bar 1$: a function (column).
In 1.2 and 1.3.4, $Q$ diagonalises $P$ and $M$ is the Jordan block. From 1.3.1 and 1.5 on, $Q$ is the transient block and $M = (I - Q)^{-1}$.
The transition function $p(i, j)$, and also a parameter of the examples (probability of a call, of a step to the right). Look for the parentheses.
Return time $\min\{n \ge 1\}$; hitting time $T_i = \min\{n \ge 0\}$; cover times $T_k$ on the circle; the book also names transient classes $T_1, \dots, T_s$.
Period $d(i)$ and degree of a vertex $d(v)$.
$\alpha_k(i)$: falling into the recurrent class $R_k$; $\alpha(t, r)$: absorbed at the point $r$; $\alpha(j)$: the gambler reaches $N$ first. Three notations for one idea.
“Any matrix satisfying (1.9) and (1.10) is irreducible” is false; counterexample $\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1/2&1/2\end{pmatrix}$. It needs all entries of $\bar\pi$ positive, or some $P^n$ all positive.

The particular solution is printed as $G_0(j) = j^2$ with general solution $j^2 + c_1 + c_2j$; it should be $-j^2$ and $-j^2 + c_1 + c_2j$. With the printed version the boundary values would give $-j(N - j) < 0$. The result (1.18), $j(N - j)$, is correct.
In (1.17) and its homogeneous equation the range is printed $j = 1, \dots, n-1$; it should be $N - 1$.
$p_{m+n+l}(i, j) \ge p_m(i, j)p_l(j, j)p_n(j, i)$ should have $p_{m+n+l}(i, i)$ on the left (the right side is a loop from $i$ to $i$). The conclusion is unaffected.
In the urn-model check a doubled plus sign is printed before $2^{-N}$.

cards.q: $X_0, X_1, X_2, \dots$ is a process with values in a finite state space $S$. (1) State the Markov property. (2) State time homogeneity and define the transition matrix $P$. (3) Which two properties make $P$ a stochastic matrix? (4) Which data determine the whole chain, and what is the probability of the path $i_0, i_1, \dots, i_n$?
pts: (1) $\mathbb{P}\{X_n = i_n \mid X_0 = i_0, \dots, X_{n-1} = i_{n-1}\} = \mathbb{P}\{X_n = i_n \mid X_{n-1} = i_{n-1}\}$: given the present state, the earlier history adds nothing.
(2) That probability does not depend on $n$: $p(i, j) = \mathbb{P}\{X_n = j \mid X_{n-1} = i\}$. $P$ is the matrix with entries $p(i, j)$, row = current state, column = next state.
(3) $0 \le p(i, j) \le 1$, and every row sums to 1: $\sum_j p(i, j) = 1$.
(4) The initial distribution $\phi(i) = \mathbb{P}\{X_0 = i\}$ and $P$: $$\mathbb{P}\{X_0 = i_0, \dots, X_n = i_n\} = \phi(i_0)p(i_0, i_1)\cdots p(i_{n-1}, i_n)$$
cards.pit: The whole history has been reduced to one matrix.

cards.q: A phone is free (state 0) or busy (state 1) in each time interval. If it is free, a call arrives during the interval with probability $p$; if it is busy, the call ends with probability $q$. (1) Write $P$, and its numbers for $p = \tfrac14$, $q = \tfrac16$. (2) Queue version: one caller may wait on hold, and the state is the number of callers 0, 1, 2. In each interval a new call arrives with probability $p$ (refused when the state is 2) and the current call ends with probability $q$, independently. Find $p(1, 0)$, $p(1, 2)$, $p(1, 1)$. (3) Write the queue matrix for $p = \tfrac14$, $q = \tfrac16$.
pts: (1) $P = \begin{pmatrix}1-p&p\\q&1-q\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}3/4&1/4\\1/6&5/6\end{pmatrix}$.
(2) $p(1, 0) = q(1-p) = \tfrac18$ (the call ends, none arrives); $p(1, 2) = p(1-q) = \tfrac{5}{24}$; $p(1, 1) = pq + (1-p)(1-q) = \tfrac{1}{24} + \tfrac{15}{24} = \tfrac23$.
(3) $P = \begin{pmatrix}3/4&1/4&0\\1/8&2/3&5/24\\0&1/6&5/6\end{pmatrix}$; every row sums to 1.
cards.pit: These two chains are the running examples for convergence: both are irreducible and aperiodic.

cards.q: (1) Define the random walk with reflecting boundary on $\{0, \dots, N\}$. (2) Define the walk with absorbing boundary. (3) Define the simple random walk on a graph. (4) How is the first a special case of the third?
pts: (2) The same in the interior, but $p(0, 0) = p(N, N) = 1$: once at 0 or $N$ the walker stays.
(3) From vertex $v$ move to one of its $d(v)$ neighbours, each with probability $\tfrac{1}{d(v)}$: $p(v, w) = \tfrac{1}{d(v)}$ if $v, w$ are adjacent, 0 otherwise.
(4) It is the simple random walk on the path $0 - 1 - \dots - N$: the end vertices have degree 1, the others degree 2.

cards.q: Markov chain with transition matrix $P$; let $p_n(i, j) = \mathbb{P}\{X_n = j \mid X_0 = i\}$. (1) State the Chapman–Kolmogorov identity and say why it holds. (2) Conclude what $p_n(i, j)$ is. (3) For the phone chain $P = \begin{pmatrix}3/4&1/4\\1/6&5/6\end{pmatrix}$ on $\{0, 1\}$ compute $p_2(0, 0)$ and $p_2(0, 1)$.
pts: (1) $p_{m+n}(i, j) = \sum_k p_m(i, k)p_n(k, j)$: split on the state $k$ at time $m$; by the Markov property the continuation from $k$ does not depend on how the chain got there.
(2) The right side is matrix multiplication, so by induction $p_n(i, j) = (P^n)_{ij}$.
(3) $p_2(0, 0) = \tfrac34 \cdot \tfrac34 + \tfrac14 \cdot \tfrac16 = \tfrac{29}{48}$; $p_2(0, 1) = \tfrac34 \cdot \tfrac14 + \tfrac14 \cdot \tfrac56 = \tfrac{19}{48}$; they add up to 1.

cards.q: A chain has transition matrix $P$ and initial distribution $\phi$, written as a row vector with $\phi(i) = \mathbb{P}\{X_0 = i\}$. (1) Give the distribution at time $n$. (2) What do a row vector times $P$ and $P$ times a column vector mean? (3) Why is $P\bar 1 = \bar 1$ for the all-ones column $\bar 1$? (4) For the phone chain $P = \begin{pmatrix}3/4&1/4\\1/6&5/6\end{pmatrix}$ on $\{0, 1\}$ find $\mathbb{P}\{X_6 = 1 \mid X_0 = 0\}$.
pts: (1) $\phi P^n$: $\mathbb{P}\{X_n = j\} = \sum_i \phi(i)p_n(i, j)$.

(2) A row vector is a distribution, and $\phi P$ is the distribution one step later. A column vector $f$ is a function on the states, and $(Pf)(i) = \sum_j p(i, j)f(j) = \mathbb{E}[f(X_1) \mid X_0 = i]$.
(3) Each row of $P$ sums to 1. So 1 is an eigenvalue of every stochastic matrix, with right eigenvector $\bar 1$.
(4) The entry $(0, 1)$ of $P^6$: $\approx 0.576$ (closed form $\tfrac35\big(1 - (\tfrac{7}{12})^6\big)$).
cards.pit: The book uses the same symbol $\bar v$ for rows and columns; read $\bar vP$ as a distribution and $P\bar v$ as a function.

cards.q: For the phone chain $\begin{pmatrix}3/4&1/4\\1/6&5/6\end{pmatrix}$ and the queue chain $\begin{pmatrix}3/4&1/4&0\\1/8&2/3&5/24\\0&1/6&5/6\end{pmatrix}$ the rows of $P^n$ become identical as $n$ grows. (1) Give the two limits. (2) What does “identical rows” say about the chain? (3) Show that a limit $\bar\pi = \lim_n \phi P^n$ must satisfy $\bar\pi = \bar\pi P$. (4) Define an invariant probability vector in the language of eigenvectors.
pts: (1) Phone: every row tends to $(\tfrac25, \tfrac35)$. Queue: to $(\tfrac{2}{11}, \tfrac{4}{11}, \tfrac{5}{11}) \approx (.182, .364, .455)$.
(2) $p_n(i, j) \to \pi(j)$ whatever the start $i$: the chain forgets where it started, and $\phi P^n \to \bar\pi$ for every initial distribution $\phi$.
(3) $\bar\pi = \lim_n \phi P^{n+1} = \big(\lim_n \phi P^n\big)P = \bar\pi P$.
(4) A left eigenvector of $P$ with eigenvalue 1 whose entries are nonnegative and sum to 1. Starting from $\bar\pi$, the distribution is $\bar\pi$ at every time.

cards.q: (1) State the three questions about invariant probability vectors that the chapter sets out to answer. (2) Give the answers for an irreducible, aperiodic chain. (3) Which answer fails for $P = \begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$? (4) Which fails for $P = I$?
pts: (1) Existence: is there a $\bar\pi$ with $\bar\pi P = \bar\pi$? Uniqueness: is there only one? Convergence: does $\phi P^n \to \bar\pi$ for every initial distribution $\phi$?
(2) Yes to all three.
(3) Convergence: $\bar\pi = (\tfrac12, \tfrac12)$ exists and is unique, but $P^n$ alternates between $I$ and $P$ (periodicity).
(4) Uniqueness: every probability vector is invariant; $P^n = I$ converges but its rows differ (reducibility).
cards.pit: Reducibility and periodicity turn out to be the only two obstacles.

cards.q: Queue chain on $\{0, 1, 2\}$ with $P = \begin{pmatrix}3/4&1/4&0\\1/8&2/3&5/24\\0&1/6&5/6\end{pmatrix}$. Solve $\bar\pi P = \bar\pi$. (1) Write the equations for column 0 and column 2. (2) Express $\pi(1)$ and $\pi(2)$ through $\pi(0)$. (3) Normalise. (4) Check column 1.
pts: (4) $\tfrac14 \cdot \tfrac{2}{11} + \tfrac23 \cdot \tfrac{4}{11} + \tfrac16 \cdot \tfrac{5}{11} = \tfrac{1}{11}\big(\tfrac12 + \tfrac83 + \tfrac56\big) = \tfrac{4}{11}$.
cards.pit: The equations of $\bar\pi P = \bar\pi$ are dependent (one is redundant); the missing equation is $\sum_j \pi(j) = 1$. Each equation reads: flow into a state = flow out of it.

cards.q: Two-state chain on $\{0, 1\}$ with $P = \begin{pmatrix}1-p&p\\q&1-q\end{pmatrix}$, $0 < p, q < 1$. (1) Find the eigenvalues and say why. (2) Find $\bar\pi$. (3) Give $P^n$ as “limit plus decaying part”. (4) Give the limit, the speed, and the numbers for $p = \tfrac14$, $q = \tfrac16$.
pts: (1) 1, because every row sums to 1; and $\lambda = 1 - p - q$, because the eigenvalues add up to the trace $(1-p) + (1-q)$.
(2) $\bar\pi = \Big(\dfrac{q}{p+q}, \dfrac{p}{p+q}\Big)$, from the balance $\pi(0)p = \pi(1)q$.
(3) $$\begin{aligned}P^n &= \frac{1}{p+q}\begin{pmatrix}q&p\\q&p\end{pmatrix}\\ &\quad + \frac{\lambda^n}{p+q}\begin{pmatrix}p&-p\\-q&q\end{pmatrix}\end{aligned}$$

(4) $|\lambda| < 1$, so the second term dies like $|\lambda|^n$ and every row tends to $\bar\pi$. Numbers: $\lambda = \tfrac{7}{12}$, $\bar\pi = (\tfrac25, \tfrac35)$, $p_n(0, 1) = \tfrac35\big(1 - (\tfrac{7}{12})^n\big)$; four more steps multiply the deviation by $(\tfrac{7}{12})^4 \approx 0.116$.
cards.pit: Convergence rests on the second eigenvalue having absolute value below 1.

cards.q: Two-state chain on $\{0, 1\}$ with $P = \begin{pmatrix}1-p&p\\q&1-q\end{pmatrix}$, now allowing $p, q \in [0, 1]$, with second eigenvalue $\lambda = 1 - p - q$. (1) What happens for $p = q = 1$? (2) For $p = q = 0$? (3) Name the two phenomena. (4) Express both through $\lambda$.
pts: (1) $P = \begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$: the chain switches every step, $P^n$ alternates between $I$ and $P$ and does not converge; $\bar\pi = (\tfrac12, \tfrac12)$ still exists and is unique.
(2) $P = I$: the two states never interact; every probability vector is invariant, so $\bar\pi$ is not unique.
(3) Periodicity and reducibility.
(4) $\lambda = -1$ in the first case ($\lambda^n$ does not decay), $\lambda = 1$ in the second (eigenvalue 1 is double). Convergence to a unique $\bar\pi$ needs $|\lambda| < 1$.
cards.pit: Both failures already show up with two states; this is why the book assumes 0 < p, q < 1.

cards.q: $P$ is a stochastic matrix. (1) State the two conditions, (1.9) and (1.10), under which $P^n$ converges to a matrix with identical rows. (2) Outline the argument using the Jordan form $P = QDQ^{-1}$. (3) Why is the limit the matrix with every row equal to $\bar\pi$? (4) What sets the speed?
pts: (1) (1.9): the left eigenvector for eigenvalue 1 can be chosen with all entries nonnegative, so it can be normalised to a probability vector $\bar\pi$. (1.10): the eigenvalue 1 is simple and every other eigenvalue has absolute value less than 1.
(2) $D = \begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&B\end{pmatrix}$ with $B$ the block of the other eigenvalues, so $B^n \to 0$ and $P^n = QD^nQ^{-1} \to Q\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}Q^{-1}$.

(3) That limit is (first column of $Q$) times (first row of $Q^{-1}$). The first column is the right eigenvector $\bar 1$, the first row the left eigenvector $\bar\pi$: the product $\bar 1\bar\pi$ has every row equal to $\bar\pi$.
(4) The largest absolute value among the other eigenvalues: the deviation shrinks essentially like $|\lambda_2|^n$.
cards.pit: The book calls the block $M$ and the diagonalising matrix $Q$ here; later $Q$ is the transient block and $M = (I - Q)^{-1}$. Different objects.

cards.q: (1) State the Perron–Frobenius theorem for a stochastic matrix all of whose entries are positive. (2) The queue matrix $\begin{pmatrix}3/4&1/4&0\\1/8&2/3&5/24\\0&1/6&5/6\end{pmatrix}$ has zero entries. How does the book get around that? (3) Why do the conclusions pass from $P^2$ to $P$? (4) State the resulting Fact.
pts: (1) 1 is a simple eigenvalue; its left eigenvector can be chosen with all entries positive; every other eigenvalue has absolute value less than 1.
(2) $P^2$ has all entries positive (e.g. entry $(0, 2)$ is $\tfrac14 \cdot \tfrac{5}{24} = \tfrac{5}{96}$), so the theorem applies to $P^2$.

(3) An eigenvalue $\mu$ of $P$ gives the eigenvalue $\mu^2$ of $P^2$ with the same eigenvector. If 1 were not simple for $P$, or $P$ had another eigenvalue with $|\mu| = 1$ (for $\mu = -1$, $\mu^2 = 1$), then $P^2$ would violate the theorem. And the left eigenvector of $P$ for 1 is the unique one of $P^2$, hence can be taken nonnegative.
(4) If for some $n$ all entries of $P^n$ are positive, then $P$ satisfies (1.9) and (1.10), so every row of $P^m$ converges to the unique invariant $\bar\pi$.
cards.pit: What remains is to say which chains have some power with all entries positive: the irreducible aperiodic ones.

cards.q: Three chains for which no power $P^n$ has all entries positive: (a) the reflecting walk on $\{0, \dots, 4\}$; (b) the absorbing walk on $\{0, \dots, 4\}$; (c) two blocks side by side, $\{1, 2\}$ with $\begin{pmatrix}1/2&1/2\\1/6&5/6\end{pmatrix}$ and $\{3, 4, 5\}$ with the queue matrix, and no transitions between the blocks. (1) What does $P^n$ do for large $n$ in (a)? (2) In (b)? (3) In (c)? (4) Name the reason in each case.
pts: (1) It alternates: for even $n$ row 0 is about $(.25, 0, .5, 0, .25)$, for odd $n$ about $(0, .5, 0, .5, 0)$. Every step changes the parity of the position.
(2) It converges but the rows differ: row 1 tends to $(.75, 0, 0, 0, .25)$, row 2 to $(.5, 0, 0, 0, .5)$, row 3 to $(.25, 0, 0, 0, .75)$; columns 1, 2, 3 vanish.
(3) It converges but the rows differ: rows 1, 2 tend to $(.25, .75, 0, 0, 0)$, rows 3, 4, 5 to $(0, 0, .182, .364, .455)$.
(4) (a) period 2; (b) the states 1, 2, 3 are transient and there are two absorbing states; (c) the chain is reducible.

cards.q: Markov chain on a finite state space. (1) Define “$i$ and $j$ communicate”, written $i \leftrightarrow j$. (2) Show that the relation is transitive. (3) Define communication classes and irreducibility. (4) Give the classes of the reflecting and of the absorbing walk on $\{0, \dots, 4\}$.
pts: (1) There are $m, n \ge 0$ with $p_m(i, j) > 0$ and $p_n(j, i) > 0$: $j$ can be reached from $i$ and $i$ from $j$.

(2) If $p_{m_1}(i, j) > 0$ and $p_{m_2}(j, k) > 0$ then $p_{m_1 + m_2}(i, k) \ge p_{m_1}(i, j)p_{m_2}(j, k) > 0$, because passing through $j$ is one way of getting from $i$ to $k$; the same for the way back. (Reflexive since $p_0(i, i) = 1$; symmetric by definition.)
(3) The equivalence classes of $\leftrightarrow$; they partition the state space. The chain is irreducible when there is only one class.

cards.q: Markov chain on a finite state space with several communication classes. (1) Define transient and recurrent classes. (2) Give a test for a finite chain. (3) Write the canonical form of $P$ and of $P^n$. (4) Say what the blocks mean and why the upper right block is 0.
pts: (1) Transient class: the chain leaves it with probability 1 and never returns. Recurrent class: the chain never leaves it.
(2) A class is recurrent exactly when it is closed (no state outside can be reached from it). There is always at least one recurrent class.

(3) Recurrent classes first, transient states last: $$P = \begin{pmatrix}\tilde P&0\\S&Q\end{pmatrix},\quad P^n = \begin{pmatrix}\tilde P^n&0\\S_n&Q^n\end{pmatrix}$$ with $\tilde P$ block diagonal with blocks $P_1, \dots, P_r$.
(4) $P_k$: transitions inside the recurrent class $R_k$ (itself a stochastic matrix). $S$: transient to recurrent. $Q$: transient to transient. Zero block: nothing leaves a recurrent class.
cards.pit: The test in part 2 is not spelled out in the book. Example: the absorbing walk has recurrent classes $\{0\}$, $\{4\}$ and the transient class $\{1, 2, 3\}$.

cards.q: The book says: “Any matrix satisfying (1.9) and (1.10) is irreducible”, where (1.9) = the left eigenvector for eigenvalue 1 can be chosen nonnegative and (1.10) = eigenvalue 1 is simple and all other eigenvalues have absolute value below 1. (1) Give a counterexample with its eigenvalues and left eigenvector. (2) Why is it reducible? (3) Give two correct statements. (4) Is “all entries of $\bar\pi$ positive” alone enough for irreducibility?
pts: (1) $P = \begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1/2&1/2\end{pmatrix}$: eigenvalues $1$ and $\tfrac12$, left eigenvector $(1, 0) \ge 0$. Both conditions hold.
(2) State 0 is absorbing and state 1 is transient: 1 cannot be reached from 0.

(3) If some $P^n$ has all entries positive, the chain is irreducible. Or: (1.9), (1.10) and all entries of $\bar\pi$ positive imply irreducibility (then $P^n \to \bar 1\bar\pi$ is eventually all positive).
(4) No: $P = I$ has the invariant vector $(\tfrac12, \tfrac12)$ and is reducible.

cards.q: Irreducible Markov chain. (1) Define the period $d(i)$ of a state. (2) Find the set of possible return times to 0 and $d(0)$ for the reflecting walk on $\{0, \dots, 4\}$ and for the queue chain with $p(0, 0) = \tfrac34$. (3) Give a quick sufficient test for period 1. (4) Which two facts give $p_{md}(i, i) > 0$ for all large $m$?
pts: (1) $d(i) = \gcd J_i$ with $J_i = \{n \ge 0 : p_n(i, i) > 0\}$.
(3) A self-loop: $p(i, i) > 0$ puts 1 in $J_i$, so $d(i) = 1$ (aperiodic).

(4) $J_i$ is closed under addition, since $p_{m+n}(i, i) \ge p_m(i, i)p_n(i, i) > 0$; and a set of nonnegative integers that is closed under addition with gcd $d$ contains all but finitely many multiples of $d$.

cards.q: Irreducible Markov chain, $J_i = \{n \ge 0 : p_n(i, i) > 0\}$, $d(i) = \gcd J_i$. Prove $d(i) = d(j)$ for two states $i, j$. (1) Choose $m, n$ and show $d(i)$ divides $m + n$. (2) For any $l \in J_j$ show $d(i)$ divides $m + l + n$. (3) Conclude.
pts: (1) Irreducible: there are $m, n$ with $p_m(i, j) > 0$, $p_n(j, i) > 0$. The loop $i \to j \to i$ gives $p_{m+n}(i, i) \ge p_m(i, j)p_n(j, i) > 0$, so $m + n \in J_i$.
(2) The loop $i \to j \to j \to i$: $p_{m+l+n}(i, i) \ge p_m(i, j)p_l(j, j)p_n(j, i) > 0$, so $m + l + n \in J_i$.
(3) Subtracting, $d(i)$ divides every $l \in J_j$, hence $d(i)$ divides $d(j)$. By symmetry $d(j)$ divides $d(i)$, so they are equal.
cards.pit: The book prints the left side of the inequality in part 2 as $p_{m+n+l}(i, j)$; it should be $p_{m+n+l}(i, i)$.

cards.q: Simple random walk on a connected graph. (1) Is it irreducible? (2) Which periods are possible, and why? (3) When is the period 2? (4) Give the period for the path $0 - 1 - 2 - 3 - 4$, for a cycle of 5 vertices and for a cycle of 4 vertices.
pts: (1) Yes: connected means every vertex can be reached from every other.
(2) 1 or 2: going to a neighbour and back is a loop of 2 steps, so $2 \in J_v$.
(3) Exactly when the graph is bipartite: the vertices split into two groups and every edge joins the two groups (equivalently, there is no loop of odd length).
(4) Path: bipartite by parity, period 2 (this is the reflecting walk). 5-cycle: loops of length 2 and 5, $\gcd = 1$, aperiodic. 4-cycle: bipartite, period 2.

cards.q: (1) State the convergence theorem for an irreducible, aperiodic chain with transition matrix $P$. (2) Which property of the powers $P^n$ is behind it? (3) Prove that property. (4) Which earlier result finishes the proof?
pts: (1) There is a unique invariant probability vector $\bar\pi$; for every initial distribution $\phi$, $\lim_{n \to \infty}\phi P^n = \bar\pi$; and $\pi(i) > 0$ for every $i$.
(2) There is an $M$ such that all entries of $P^n$ are positive for every $n \ge M$.

(3) Aperiodic: there is $M(i)$ with $p_n(i, i) > 0$ for all $n \ge M(i)$. Irreducible: there is $m(i, j)$ with $p_{m(i,j)}(i, j) > 0$. Loop at $i$, then go to $j$: $p_{n + m(i,j)}(i, j) \ge p_n(i, i)p_{m(i,j)}(i, j) > 0$ for $n \ge M(i)$. Take $M = \max_{i,j}\big(M(i) + m(i, j)\big)$, a maximum over finitely many pairs.
(4) The Fact: some power with all entries positive gives (1.9) and (1.10), hence $P^n \to \bar 1\bar\pi$.

cards.q: Reducible chain with recurrent classes $R_1, \dots, R_r$, each aperiodic; $\bar\pi^k$ is the invariant distribution of $R_k$ and $\alpha_k(i)$ the probability that the chain started at the transient state $i$ ends up in $R_k$. Give $\lim_n p_n(i, j)$ (1) for $i \in R_k$; (2) for $j$ transient; (3) for $i$ transient and $j \in R_k$. (4) Describe all invariant distributions and the multiplicity of the eigenvalue 1. (5) Evaluate $\lim_n p_n(1, 0)$ for the absorbing walk on $\{0, \dots, 4\}$.
pts: (1) $\pi^k(j)$ if $j \in R_k$, and 0 otherwise.
(3) $\alpha_k(i)\pi^k(j)$: first fall into $R_k$, then settle into equilibrium there.
(4) Every mixture $c_1\bar\pi^1 + \dots + c_r\bar\pi^r$ with $c_k \ge 0$, $\sum c_k = 1$; not unique when $r \ge 2$. The eigenvalue 1 has multiplicity $r$.
(5) $R_1 = \{0\}$ with all mass at 0, and from 1 the walk ends at 0 with probability $\tfrac34$: the limit is $\tfrac34$.
cards.pit: $\lim\phi P^n$ exists but depends on $\phi$.

cards.q: Irreducible chain with period $d > 1$. (1) Describe the structure of the state space. (2) Which eigenvalues have absolute value 1? (3) What stays true and what fails? (4) For the reflecting walk on $\{0, \dots, 4\}$ give the eigenvalues, $\bar\pi$, the behaviour of $p_n(0, 0)$ and the meaning of $\pi(0)$.
pts: (1) The states split into $d$ groups $A_1, \dots, A_d$ and the chain cycles $A_1 \to A_2 \to \dots \to A_d \to A_1$.
(2) The $d$ complex roots of $z^d = 1$, each a simple eigenvalue.

(3) True: a unique invariant $\bar\pi$ with all entries positive. Fails: $\phi P^n$ does not converge; it cycles through $d$ distributions whose average is $\bar\pi$: $$\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1d\big[\phi P^{n+1} + \dots + \phi P^{n+d}\big] = \bar\pi$$

(4) Eigenvalues $1, -1, 0, \pm\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$; $\bar\pi = (\tfrac18, \tfrac14, \tfrac14, \tfrac14, \tfrac18)$; $p_n(0, 0) \to \tfrac14$ along even $n$ and is 0 for odd $n$; $\pi(0) = \tfrac18$ is the average of the two, the long-run fraction of time at 0.
cards.pit: Same shape as the two-state chain, limit plus (second eigenvalue)$^n$ times a deviation, but the second eigenvalue is $-1$ and its term never decays.

cards.q: Compare three kinds of finite chains: (a) irreducible and aperiodic; (b) irreducible with period $d > 1$; (c) reducible with aperiodic recurrent classes. (1) Does $\bar\pi$ exist, and is it unique? (2) Does $P^n$ converge? (3) What does $\pi(j)$ mean? (4) Give one example of each.
pts: (1) It exists in all three. Unique in (a) and (b); in (c) there is one per recurrent class and every mixture of them is invariant.
(2) (a) yes, every row tends to $\bar\pi$; (b) no, it cycles with period $d$; (c) yes, but the rows differ.
(3) (a) limiting probability and long-run fraction of time; (b) long-run fraction of time only; (c) $\lim p_n(i, j) = \alpha_k(i)\pi^k(j)$ depends on the start.
(4) (a) phone chain, queue; (b) reflecting walk; (c) absorbing walk.

cards.q: Irreducible chain with invariant distribution $\bar\pi$; $Y(j, n) = \sum_{m=0}^n I\{X_m = j\}$ counts the visits to $j$ up to time $n$. (1) Express $\mathbb{E}[Y(j, n) \mid X_0 = i]$ through the $p_m(i, j)$. (2) Give the limit of $\mathbb{E}[Y(j, n) \mid X_0 = i]/(n+1)$ and the reason for an aperiodic chain. (3) Why does it also hold for a periodic chain? (4) State the interpretation.
pts: (1) $\sum_{m=0}^n p_m(i, j)$: the expectation of an indicator is a probability.
(2) $\pi(j)$: every term $p_m(i, j)$ tends to $\pi(j)$, so the average does too.
(3) The terms do not converge, but their averages over $d$ consecutive steps tend to $\pi(j)$, so the long-run average does as well.
(4) $\pi(j)$ is the long-run fraction of time spent at $j$, for every irreducible chain.

cards.q: Irreducible chain with invariant distribution $\bar\pi$, started at $X_0 = i$; the return time is $T = \min\{n \ge 1 : X_n = i\}$. (1) State the formula for $\mathbb{E}(T)$. (2) Give the book's heuristic argument. (3) What is missing for a rigorous proof? (4) Apply it to the state 0 of the reflecting walk on $\{0, \dots, 4\}$, where $\bar\pi = (\tfrac18, \tfrac14, \tfrac14, \tfrac14, \tfrac18)$.
pts: (1) $\mathbb{E}(T) = \dfrac{1}{\pi(i)}$.

(2) The successive return times $T_1, T_2, \dots$ are independent copies of $T$ (the chain starts afresh at each return), so $k$ returns take about $k\,\mathbb{E}(T)$ steps. In $n$ steps there are about $n\pi(i)$ visits to $i$. With $n = k\,\mathbb{E}(T)$: $k \approx k\,\mathbb{E}(T)\pi(i)$.
(3) That $\mathbb{E}(T) < \infty$ (a geometric tail bound) and the restart at a random time. A rigorous proof counts the expected visits to each state during one return cycle.
cards.pit: The starting moment does not count: $n \ge 1$ in the definition of $T$.

cards.q: Two-state chain on $\{0, 1\}$ with $P = \begin{pmatrix}1-p&p\\q&1-q\end{pmatrix}$, $0 < p, q < 1$, started at 0; $T$ is the return time to 0. (1) Find $\mathbb{P}\{T = 1\}$ and $\mathbb{P}\{T \ge n\}$ for $n \ge 2$. (2) State the tail-sum formula for the mean and say where it comes from. (3) Compute $\mathbb{E}(T)$. (4) Compare with Kac's formula and give the numbers for $p = \tfrac14$, $q = \tfrac16$.
pts: (1) $\mathbb{P}\{T = 1\} = 1 - p$. For $n \ge 2$: go to 1, then stay there for $n - 2$ steps, $\mathbb{P}\{T \ge n\} = p(1-q)^{n-2}$.

(2) For $Y$ with values in $\{0, 1, 2, \dots\}$: $\mathbb{E}(Y) = \sum_{k \ge 1}\mathbb{P}\{Y \ge k\}$. Write $n\,\mathbb{P}\{Y = n\}$ as $n$ copies of $\mathbb{P}\{Y = n\}$ and swap the order of summation.
(3) $\mathbb{E}(T) = 1 + \sum_{n \ge 2}p(1-q)^{n-2} = 1 + \dfrac pq = \dfrac{p+q}{q}$.
(4) $\pi(0) = \tfrac{q}{p+q}$, so $\mathbb{E}(T) = 1/\pi(0)$. Numbers: $1 + \tfrac{1/4}{1/6} = \tfrac52$; from state 1 the mean return time is $1/\pi(1) = \tfrac53$.

cards.q: Two-state chain on $\{0, 1\}$ that switches state with probability $p$ at each step (the same $p$ from both states); $T$ is the return time to 0. (1) Give $\bar\pi$ and $\mathbb{E}(T)$. (2) Describe $T$ for $p = 0.9$ and for $p = 0.1$. (3) Derive $\operatorname{Var}(T)$ and evaluate it in both cases. (4) State the lesson.
pts: (1) $\bar\pi = (\tfrac12, \tfrac12)$ and $\mathbb{E}(T) = 2$ for every $p$.
(2) $p = 0.9$: the chain switches almost every step, $T$ is usually 2. $p = 0.1$: $T$ is usually 1, occasionally very large.

(3) $T = 1$ with probability $1 - p$; otherwise $T = 1 + G$ with $G$ geometric on $\{1, 2, \dots\}$ with parameter $p$. $\mathbb{E}(T^2) = (1-p) + p\big(1 + \tfrac2p + \tfrac{2-p}{p^2}\big) = 2 + \tfrac2p$, so $\operatorname{Var}(T) = \dfrac{2(1-p)}{p}$: $\tfrac29 \approx 0.22$ against $18$.
(4) $\bar\pi$ determines the mean return time only, not the distribution of $T$.

cards.q: A chain has transient states; $Q$ is the part of $P$ that goes from transient states to transient states. (1) Why does $Q^n \to 0$, and what follows for $I - Q$? (2) Define $M$ and state what $M_{ji}$ means. (3) Prove it. (4) What do the row sums of $M$ mean?
pts: (1) For transient $i, j$: $p_n(j, i) = (Q^n)_{ji}$, and transient states are eventually left for good. So all eigenvalues of $Q$ have absolute value below 1 and $I - Q$ is invertible.
(2) $M = (I - Q)^{-1}$; $M_{ji}$ is the expected number of visits to $i$ for the chain started at $j$ (the visit at time 0 counts).
(3) With $Y_i = \sum_{n \ge 0}I\{X_n = i\}$: $\mathbb{E}(Y_i \mid X_0 = j) = \sum_{n \ge 0}(Q^n)_{ji} = (I + Q + Q^2 + \dots)_{ji}$, and $(I + Q + \dots + Q^n)(I - Q) = I - Q^{n+1} \to I$.
(4) $\sum_i M_{ji}$ is the expected number of steps spent among the transient states starting from $j$, because each such step is spent at exactly one transient state. In vector form: $M\bar 1$.
cards.pit: It is the matrix version of $1 + x + x^2 + \dots = \tfrac{1}{1-x}$ for $|x| < 1$.

cards.q: Consider the absorbing random walk on $\{0, 1, 2, 3, 4\}$ (from 1, 2, 3 one step left or right with probability $\tfrac12$ each; $p(0, 0) = p(4, 4) = 1$); the transient states are 1, 2, 3. (1) Write $Q$. (2) Give $M = (I - Q)^{-1}$. (3) Read off the expected number of visits to 3 and to 1 for the walk started at 1. (4) Give the expected number of steps before absorption from 1, 2 and 3.
pts: (3) $M_{13} = \tfrac12$; $M_{11} = \tfrac32$ (the start counts, so it is at least 1).
(4) The row sums: $3, 4, 3$.
cards.pit: Check one row of $M(I - Q) = I$: $(\tfrac32, 1, \tfrac12)$ against the columns of $I - Q$ gives $\tfrac32 - \tfrac12 = 1$, $-\tfrac34 + 1 - \tfrac14 = 0$, $-\tfrac12 + \tfrac12 = 0$.

cards.q: An irreducible chain has no transient states, but the mean number of steps from $j$ to $i \ne j$ is wanted. (1) Describe the trick. (2) Give the formula. (3) For the reflecting random walk on $\{0, 1, 2, 3, 4\}$ (from 1, 2, 3 one step left or right with probability $\tfrac12$ each; $p(0, 1) = p(4, 3) = 1$) and target 0, write $Q$ and give $M$ and $M\bar 1$. (4) Check against Kac's formula, using $\pi(0) = \tfrac18$.
pts: (1) Make $i$ absorbing ($p(i, i) = 1$). All other states become transient, and the steps from $j$ to $i$ are the time the modified chain spends among its transient states.
(2) With $T_i = \min\{n \ge 0 : X_n = i\}$: $\mathbb{E}(T_i \mid X_0 = j) = \sum_{k \ne i}M_{jk}$, the component $j$ of $M\bar 1$.

(3) States $1, 2, 3, 4$: $$Q = \begin{pmatrix}0&\frac12&0&0\\\frac12&0&\frac12&0\\0&\frac12&0&\frac12\\0&0&1&0\end{pmatrix},\quad M = \begin{pmatrix}2&2&2&1\\2&4&4&2\\2&4&6&3\\2&4&6&4\end{pmatrix}$$ $M\bar 1 = (7, 12, 15, 16)$: from 4 to 0 takes 16 steps on average.
(4) From 0 the first step goes to 1, and from 1 to 0 takes 7 steps: $1 + 7 = 8 = 1/\pi(0)$.
cards.pit: The last row of $Q$ is $(0, 0, 1, 0)$: at 4 the walker must bounce back to 3.

cards.q: For a state $i$ of an irreducible chain: (1) define the return time $T$ and the hitting time $T_i$; (2) give their values for a chain started at $i$; (3) say how each mean is computed; (4) give the relation between them.
pts: (1) $T = \min\{n \ge 1 : X_n = i\}$ for the chain started at $i$; $T_i = \min\{n \ge 0 : X_n = i\}$ from any start.
(3) $\mathbb{E}_i(T) = 1/\pi(i)$ (Kac). $\mathbb{E}_j(T_i)$ is the component $j$ of $M\bar 1$ after making $i$ absorbing.
(4) $\mathbb{E}_i(T) = 1 + \sum_j p(i, j)\,\mathbb{E}_j(T_i)$: take one step, then the hitting time from where it lands.

cards.q: The recurrent classes of a chain are absorbing states $r_1, \dots, r_k$; $\alpha(t, r)$ is the probability that the chain started at the transient state $t$ is absorbed at $r$. (1) Give the boundary values. (2) Write the first-step equation. (3) Put it in matrix form and solve. (4) For the absorbing random walk on $\{0, 1, 2, 3, 4\}$ (from 1, 2, 3 one step left or right with probability $\tfrac12$ each; $p(0, 0) = p(4, 4) = 1$) give $S$ and the absorption probabilities.
pts: (1) $\alpha(r, r) = 1$ and $\alpha(r', r) = 0$ for another absorbing state $r'$.
(2) $\alpha(t, r) = \sum_z p(t, z)\alpha(z, r) = p(t, r) + \sum_{z\ \text{transient}}p(t, z)\alpha(z, r)$: landing on $r$ counts 1, landing on another absorbing state counts 0.
(3) $A = S + QA$, so $A = (I - Q)^{-1}S = MS$, where $S$ holds the transition probabilities from transient to absorbing states.
(4) Columns 0 and 4, rows 1, 2, 3: $$S = \begin{pmatrix}1/2&0\\0&0\\0&1/2\end{pmatrix},\quad MS = \begin{pmatrix}3/4&1/4\\1/2&1/2\\1/4&3/4\end{pmatrix}$$ Each row sums to 1.
cards.pit: A recurrent class with several states is first collapsed into one absorbing point.

cards.q: A gambler has $j$ dollars, $0 \le j \le N$. Each round she wins 1 with probability $p$ and loses 1 with probability $1 - p$; the game stops at 0 or $N$. Let $\alpha(j)$ be the probability of reaching $N$ before 0. (1) Write the equation and the boundary values. (2) Solve for $p \ne \tfrac12$. (3) Solve for $p = \tfrac12$. (4) Give $\alpha(1), \alpha(2), \alpha(3)$ for $N = 4$ with $p = \tfrac12$ and with $p = \tfrac23$.
pts: (1) $\alpha(j) = (1-p)\alpha(j-1) + p\alpha(j+1)$ for $0 < j < N$; $\alpha(0) = 0$, $\alpha(N) = 1$.

(2) Trying $x^j$: $px^2 - x + (1-p) = 0$, roots $1$ and $\rho = \tfrac{1-p}{p}$. $\alpha(j) = c_1 + c_2\rho^j$ with $c_1 + c_2 = 0$ and $c_1 + c_2\rho^N = 1$: $$\alpha(j) = \frac{1 - \rho^j}{1 - \rho^N}$$
(3) Double root 1: $\alpha(j) = c_1 + c_2j$ with $c_1 = 0$, $c_2N = 1$: $\alpha(j) = \dfrac jN$.
(4) $p = \tfrac12$: $\tfrac14, \tfrac12, \tfrac34$ (the second column of $MS$ for the absorbing walk). $p = \tfrac23$, $\rho = \tfrac12$: $\tfrac{8}{15}, \tfrac45, \tfrac{14}{15}$.

cards.q: Gambler's ruin with win probability $p$ per round, starting capital $j$ and target $N$; $\rho = \tfrac{1-p}{p}$ and the probability of reaching $N$ before 0 is $\tfrac{1 - \rho^j}{1 - \rho^N}$ for $p \ne \tfrac12$ and $\tfrac jN$ for $p = \tfrac12$. Let $N \to \infty$ with $j$ fixed. (1) What happens for $p = \tfrac12$? (2) For $p < \tfrac12$? (3) For $p > \tfrac12$? (4) Evaluate the case $j = 1$, $p = \tfrac23$.
pts: (1) $\tfrac jN \to 0$: against a house with unlimited capital, ruin is certain even in a fair game.
(2) $\rho > 1$, the denominator $1 - \rho^N \to -\infty$ and the probability tends to 0.
(3) $\rho < 1$, $\rho^N \to 0$ and the probability tends to $1 - \rho^j > 0$: a positive chance of never being ruined.
(4) $1 - \tfrac12 = \tfrac12$.

cards.q: Fair gambler's ruin on $\{0, \dots, N\}$ ($p = \tfrac12$, the game stops at 0 or $N$); $G(j)$ is the expected number of rounds starting from $j$. (1) Write the equation and the boundary values. (2) Find a particular solution and check it. (3) Write the general solution and fix the constants. (4) Give the result, check it for $N = 4$ and say what it shows.
pts: (1) $G(j) = 1 + \tfrac12G(j-1) + \tfrac12G(j+1)$ for $j = 1, \dots, N-1$; $G(0) = G(N) = 0$. The 1 is the round just played.
(3) $G(j) = -j^2 + c_1 + c_2j$ (particular solution plus the homogeneous $c_1 + c_2j$); $G(0) = 0$ gives $c_1 = 0$, $G(N) = 0$ gives $c_2 = N$.
(4) $G(j) = j(N - j)$. For $N = 4$: $3, 4, 3$, the row sums of $M$ for the absorbing walk. From the middle it takes $N^2/4$ rounds: the time grows like the square of the distance.
cards.pit: The book prints the particular solution as $j^2$ (wrong sign: substituting gives $j^2 + 2$) and the range as $n - 1$ instead of $N - 1$. The final formula $j(N - j)$ is correct.

cards.q: For a chain with absorbing states, three quantities are computed by “take one step”: $f$ = probability of being absorbed at a chosen target, $g$ = expected number of steps until absorption, $h$ = expected number of visits to a transient state $i$. Compare them: (1) boundary values; (2) one-step equations at a transient state $x$; (3) matrix forms; (4) values for the absorbing walk on $\{0, \dots, 4\}$ started at 1 (target 0; visits to 3).
pts: (1) $f = 1$ at the target and 0 at the other absorbing states; $g = 0$ and $h = 0$ at all absorbing states.
(2) $f(x) = \sum_y p(x, y)f(y)$; $g(x) = 1 + \sum_y p(x, y)g(y)$; $h(x) = I\{x = i\} + \sum_y p(x, y)h(y)$.
(3) $MS$; $M\bar 1$; column $i$ of $M$. The same $M = (I - Q)^{-1}$, only the right-hand factor differs.
(4) $\tfrac34$; 3 steps; $\tfrac12$ visit.
cards.pit: What is added in the equation: nothing, 1 for every step, 1 for every visit to i.

cards.q: Simple random walk on a connected graph with $e$ edges; $d(v)$ is the degree of the vertex $v$. (1) Give the invariant distribution. (2) Why is it a probability vector? (3) Verify invariance. (4) Apply it to the path $0 - 1 - 2 - 3 - 4$.
pts: (2) Every edge has two endpoints, so $\sum_v d(v) = 2e$.
(3) Probability flows into $w$ only from its neighbours, each neighbour $v$ sending $\tfrac{1}{d(v)}$ of its mass: $\sum_{v \sim w}\dfrac{d(v)}{2e}\cdot\dfrac{1}{d(v)} = \dfrac{d(w)}{2e}$.
(4) Degrees $(1, 2, 2, 2, 1)$, $e = 4$: $\bar\pi = (\tfrac18, \tfrac14, \tfrac14, \tfrac14, \tfrac18)$, the invariant distribution of the reflecting walk in one line.
cards.pit: The higher the degree, the more ways in, and the larger the share of time.

cards.q: Random walk on a circle of $N$ points: each step goes to one of the two neighbours with probability $\tfrac12$; start at 0. $T_k$ is the first time $k$ different points have been visited ($T_1 = 0$, $T_2 = 1$) and $r(k) = \mathbb{E}[T_k - T_{k-1}]$. (1) Where is the walker at time $T_{k-1}$? (2) Write an equation for $r(k)$. (3) Solve it. (4) Give $\mathbb{E}[T_N]$ and its value for $N = 5$.
pts: (1) The visited points form an arc of $k - 1$ points and the walker stands at one end of it (it has just stepped onto a new point).

(2) With probability $\tfrac12$ the next step goes outward to a new point. Otherwise it goes inward, needs on average $1 \cdot (k - 2 - 1) = k - 3$ more steps to get back to an end of the arc (duration of a fair game on $\{0, \dots, k-2\}$ from 1), and then starts over: $r(k) = 1 + \tfrac12\big[(k - 3) + r(k)\big]$.
cards.pit: The last point to be visited is uniformly distributed on $\{1, \dots, N-1\}$.

cards.q: An urn holds $N$ balls, each red or green. Each period one ball is drawn at random; with probability $\tfrac12$ it is replaced by a ball of the other colour, otherwise it is put back. $X_n$ is the number of red balls. (1) Give the transition probabilities. (2) Is the chain irreducible and aperiodic? (3) Give the invariant distribution and the reason. (4) For $N = 4$ give $\bar\pi$ and the mean time to return to “no red balls”.
pts: (1) $p(j, j+1) = \dfrac{N-j}{2N}$ (draw a green ball and switch it), $p(j, j-1) = \dfrac{j}{2N}$, $p(j, j) = \tfrac12$.
(2) Yes: neighbouring states communicate, and the self-loops $p(j, j) = \tfrac12$ make it aperiodic.
(3) Binomial: $\pi(j) = \dbinom Nj2^{-N}$. In the long run the colour of each ball is like an independent fair coin flip.
(4) $\bar\pi = \tfrac{1}{16}(1, 4, 6, 4, 1)$; by Kac's formula $1/\pi(0) = 2^N = 16$ steps.
cards.pit: Check of one component for $N = 4$: $\tfrac{4}{16}\cdot\tfrac38 + \tfrac{6}{16}\cdot\tfrac12 + \tfrac{4}{16}\cdot\tfrac38 = \tfrac{6}{16} = \pi(2)$.

cards.q: A cell contains $N$ particles, $j$ of type I and $N - j$ of type II. It duplicates into $2j$ and $2(N - j)$ particles, and the next cell receives $N$ of these $2N$ chosen at random. (1) Give the probability $p(j, k)$ that the next cell has $k$ particles of type I. (2) Which states are absorbing? (3) Guess and verify the probability $\alpha(j)$ of ending with all particles of type I. (4) Why does verifying settle it?
pts: (1) Hypergeometric: $p(j, k) = \dbinom{2j}{k}\dbinom{2N - 2j}{N - k}\Big/\dbinom{2N}{N}$.
(2) 0 and $N$: once all particles are of one type nothing changes.

(3) $\alpha(j) = \tfrac jN$, because the expected fraction of type I does not change from one generation to the next: $\sum_k p(j, k)\tfrac kN = \tfrac1N \cdot N \cdot \tfrac{2j}{2N} = \tfrac jN$ (mean of the hypergeometric distribution), and $\alpha(0) = 0$, $\alpha(N) = 1$.
(4) The equation $A = S + QA$ has exactly one solution because $I - Q$ is invertible.
cards.pit: Example for $N = 4$: $p(2, 2) = \tbinom42\tbinom42/\tbinom84 = \tfrac{36}{70} = \tfrac{18}{35}$.

cards.q: A deck of $n$ cards is shuffled by choosing one card at random (probability $\tfrac1n$ each) and putting it on top. The states are the $n!$ orderings. (1) Why is the chain irreducible? (2) Why aperiodic? (3) Give the invariant distribution and the reason. (4) A deck of 52 cards is shuffled this way once a second. How long, on average, until the original order returns?
pts: (1) Any ordering can be built by moving cards to the top one at a time, starting with the card that should end up at the bottom.
(2) Choosing the top card leaves the order unchanged: a self-loop.

(3) Uniform, $\tfrac{1}{n!}$: each ordering is reached from exactly $n$ orderings (put its top card back into position $1, \dots, n$), each with probability $\tfrac1n$, so every column of $P$ also sums to 1 and the uniform vector satisfies $\bar\pi P = \bar\pi$.
(4) Kac: $1/\pi = 52!$ seconds $\approx 8.07 \times 10^{67}$ seconds $\approx 2.56 \times 10^{60}$ years.
cards.pit: How many shuffles are enough to mix the deck is a different question that the book does not treat.

cards.q: A newspaper is added to a pile every morning. Each afternoon, with probability $\tfrac13$, the whole pile is thrown out; and whenever the pile reaches 5 papers it is thrown out for certain. $X_n$ is the number of papers in the pile in the evening. (1) Give the states and the transition probabilities. (2) Find $\bar\pi$. (3) Find the long-run mean number of papers. (4) Find the mean time to return from 0 to 0.
pts: (1) States $0, \dots, 4$; $p(i, 0) = \tfrac13$ and $p(i, i+1) = \tfrac23$ for $i \le 3$; $p(4, 0) = 1$.
(2) Column $j \ge 1$: $\pi(j) = \tfrac23\pi(j-1)$, so $\bar\pi \propto (1, \tfrac23, \tfrac49, \tfrac{8}{27}, \tfrac{16}{81})$: $\bar\pi = \tfrac{1}{211}(81, 54, 36, 24, 16)$.
(4) Kac: $\tfrac{211}{81} \approx 2.60$ days.

cards.q: Chain on $\{0, 1\}$ with $P = \begin{pmatrix}1/3&2/3\\3/4&1/4\end{pmatrix}$ and $X_0 = 0$. (1) Find the distributions of $X_1$ and $X_2$. (2) Find $\mathbb{P}\{X_3 = 1\}$. (3) Find $\bar\pi$ and the second eigenvalue, and compare with part 2.
pts: (1) $(\tfrac13, \tfrac23)$; then $(\tfrac19 + \tfrac12, \tfrac29 + \tfrac16) = (\tfrac{11}{18}, \tfrac{7}{18})$.
(2) $\tfrac{11}{18}\cdot\tfrac23 + \tfrac{7}{18}\cdot\tfrac14 = \tfrac{88 + 21}{216} = \tfrac{109}{216} \approx 0.505$.

(3) $\bar\pi = (\tfrac{9}{17}, \tfrac{8}{17})$ and $\lambda = 1 - \tfrac23 - \tfrac34 = -\tfrac{5}{12}$. Since $\lambda < 0$ the probabilities oscillate around the limit: $p_n(0, 1) = \tfrac{8}{17}\big(1 - \lambda^n\big)$, which is $\tfrac{109}{216}$ at $n = 3$, above $\tfrac{8}{17} \approx 0.471$.

cards.q: Chain on $\{1, 2, 3\}$ with $P = \begin{pmatrix}.4&.2&.4\\.6&0&.4\\.2&.5&.3\end{pmatrix}$. (1) Why does $P^n$ converge to a matrix with identical rows? (2) Solve $\bar\pi P = \bar\pi$. (3) Give the long-run probability of state 1. (4) Starting at 2, how many steps on average until the chain is back at 2?
pts: (1) The chain is irreducible (all states communicate, e.g. $1 \to 2 \to 1$ and $1 \to 3 \to 2$) and aperiodic ($p(1, 1) = .4 > 0$).
cards.pit: Check of column 1: $.4 \cdot 25 + .6 \cdot 17 + .2 \cdot 24 = 25$.

cards.q: Chain on $\{0, \dots, 5\}$ with $$P = \begin{pmatrix}.5&.5&0&0&0&0\\.3&.7&0&0&0&0\\0&0&.1&0&.9&0\\.25&.25&0&0&.25&.25\\0&0&.7&0&.3&0\\0&.2&0&.2&.2&.4\end{pmatrix}$$ (1) Find the communication classes and say which are recurrent. (2) Find $\lim_n p_n(0, 0)$. (3) Find the probability that the chain started at 5 ends up in $\{0, 1\}$. (4) Find $\lim_n p_n(5, 0)$.
pts: (1) $\{0, 1\}$ and $\{2, 4\}$ are closed, hence recurrent. $\{3, 5\}$ communicate ($3 \to 5$, $5 \to 3$) but leak out ($3 \to 0$): transient.
(2) Inside $\{0, 1\}$ the chain is $\begin{pmatrix}.5&.5\\.3&.7\end{pmatrix}$ with $.5\pi(0) = .3\pi(1)$: $\bar\pi = (\tfrac38, \tfrac58)$, so the limit is $\tfrac38$.

(3) In the order $3, 5$: $Q = \begin{pmatrix}0&.25\\.2&.4\end{pmatrix}$, one-step probabilities into $\{0, 1\}$: $(.5, .2)$. $(I - Q)^{-1} = \tfrac{1}{.55}\begin{pmatrix}.6&.25\\.2&1\end{pmatrix}$, which gives $(\tfrac{7}{11}, \tfrac{6}{11})$: from 5 it is $\tfrac{6}{11}$.
(4) $\tfrac{6}{11}\cdot\tfrac38 = \tfrac{9}{44} \approx 0.205$.
cards.pit: A reducible chain is always handled in two stages: which recurrent class absorbs the chain, then the long-run share inside that class; multiply.

cards.q: Simple random walk on the graph with vertices $A, B, C, D, E$ and edges $AB, AC, AD, BC, BE, DE$ (each step goes to a uniformly chosen neighbour). (1) Find the degrees and $\bar\pi$. (2) Starting at $A$, find the expected number of steps until the walk is back at $A$. (3) Starting at $B$, find the probability of reaching $A$ before $C$.
pts: (1) Degrees $(3, 3, 2, 2, 2)$ for $A, B, C, D, E$ and $e = 6$: $\bar\pi = (\tfrac14, \tfrac14, \tfrac16, \tfrac16, \tfrac16)$.

(3) $f(A) = 1$, $f(C) = 0$; $f(B) = \tfrac13\big(1 + 0 + f(E)\big)$, $f(E) = \tfrac12\big(f(B) + f(D)\big)$, $f(D) = \tfrac12\big(1 + f(E)\big)$. Then $f(E) = \tfrac23f(B) + \tfrac13$ and $f(B) = \tfrac49 + \tfrac29f(B)$: $f(B) = \tfrac47$.

cards.q: Simple random walk on the graph with vertices $A, B, C, D, E$ and edges $AB, AC, AD, BC, BE, DE$ (each step goes to a uniformly chosen neighbour). Make $A$ absorbing. (1) Write the one-step equations for $g(x)$ = expected number of steps from $x$ to $A$. (2) Solve for $g(C)$. (3) Starting at $C$, find the expected number of visits to $B$ before the walk reaches $A$.
pts: (1) $g(B) = 1 + \tfrac13\big(g(C) + g(E)\big)$, $g(C) = 1 + \tfrac12g(B)$, $g(D) = 1 + \tfrac12g(E)$, $g(E) = 1 + \tfrac12\big(g(B) + g(D)\big)$.

(3) $h(B) = 1 + \tfrac13\big(h(C) + h(E)\big)$, $h(C) = \tfrac12h(B)$, $h(D) = \tfrac12h(E)$, $h(E) = \tfrac12\big(h(B) + h(D)\big)$. Then $h(E) = \tfrac23h(B)$, $h(B) = 1 + \tfrac{7}{18}h(B) = \tfrac{18}{11}$ and $h(C) = \tfrac{9}{11}$.
cards.pit: The two systems differ only in where the 1 is added: at every state for steps, at B only for visits to B.

cards.q: Chain on $\{1, \dots, 5\}$: from 1 go to 2 with probability $\tfrac13$ or to 3 with probability $\tfrac23$; from 2 go to 4 with probability $\tfrac14$ or to 5 with probability $\tfrac34$; from 3 go to 4 or 5 with probability $\tfrac12$ each; from 4 and from 5 go to 1. (1) Is the chain irreducible, and what is its period? (2) Give the distribution of the return time to 1 and deduce $\pi(1)$ without solving equations. (3) Find $\bar\pi$ and the mean return time to 2. (4) Give $p_{1000}(2, 1)$, $p_{1000}(2, 2)$ and approximately $p_{1000}(2, 4)$.
pts: (1) $1 \to \{2, 3\} \to \{4, 5\} \to 1$: irreducible, and every loop has a length divisible by 3, so $d = 3$.
(2) The return time is always exactly 3, so by Kac's formula $\pi(1) = \tfrac13$.
(3) $\pi(2) = \tfrac13\pi(1) = \tfrac19$, $\pi(3) = \tfrac29$, $\pi(4) = \tfrac14\cdot\tfrac19 + \tfrac12\cdot\tfrac29 = \tfrac{5}{36}$, $\pi(5) = \tfrac{7}{36}$. Mean return time to 2: $9$.
(4) $1000 \equiv 1 \pmod 3$, so at time 1000 the chain started in $\{2, 3\}$ is in $\{4, 5\}$: the first two are 0, and $p_{1000}(2, 4) \approx 3\pi(4) = \tfrac{5}{12}$.
cards.pit: Periodicity only breaks the convergence of p_n(i, j); the invariant distribution and Kac's formula are unaffected.

cards.q: Simple random walk on the complete graph with $N$ vertices: each step moves to one of the other $N - 1$ vertices, chosen uniformly. (1) Give the distribution and the mean of the return time $T$ to the starting vertex. (2) Give the mean number of steps from vertex 2 to vertex 1. (3) Give the expected time until every vertex has been visited. (4) Evaluate all three for $N = 4$.
pts: (1) The first step leaves; afterwards each step returns with probability $\tfrac{1}{N-1}$. So $T - 1$ is geometric with parameter $\tfrac{1}{N-1}$ and $\mathbb{E}(T) = 1 + (N - 1) = N$, in agreement with the uniform $\bar\pi$.
(2) Geometric with parameter $\tfrac{1}{N-1}$: mean $N - 1$.
(3) While $m$ vertices are unvisited each step finds a new one with probability $\tfrac{m}{N-1}$: $\sum_{m=1}^{N-1}\dfrac{N-1}{m} = (N-1)\Big(1 + \tfrac12 + \dots + \tfrac{1}{N-1}\Big)$.

cards.q: A fair coin is flipped until four heads in a row have appeared. (1) Set up a Markov chain. (2) Write the equations for the expected number of flips. (3) Solve them. (4) Give the answer for $k$ heads in a row.
pts: (1) State = current run of heads, $0, \dots, 4$; from $i < 4$ go to $i + 1$ or back to 0 with probability $\tfrac12$ each; 4 is absorbing.

cards.q: Irreducible chain with $N$ states and a target state $j$. Show that there are $C < \infty$ and $\rho < 1$ with $\mathbb{P}\{X_m \ne j,\ m = 0, \dots, n \mid X_0 = i\} \le C\rho^n$ for all $i$ and $n$, and that return times have finite mean. (1) Find a uniform chance of hitting $j$. (2) Use blocks of steps. (3) Identify $C$ and $\rho$. (4) Conclude.
pts: (1) By irreducibility, from every state $i$ there is a path to $j$ of at most $N$ steps, so the chain started at $i$ visits $j$ within $N$ steps with some probability $\delta_i > 0$. Put $\delta = \min_i\delta_i > 0$, a minimum of finitely many positive numbers.
(2) By the Markov property at the times $N, 2N, \dots$, whatever the state then: $\mathbb{P}\{\text{no visit to } j \text{ in the first } kN \text{ steps}\} \le (1 - \delta)^k$.
(3) For $kN \le n < (k+1)N$ the probability is at most $(1 - \delta)^k \le (1 - \delta)^{n/N - 1}$: take $\rho = (1 - \delta)^{1/N}$ and $C = \tfrac{1}{1 - \delta}$.
(4) $\mathbb{E}(T) = \sum_{n \ge 1}\mathbb{P}\{T \ge n\}$ is bounded by a geometric series, hence finite.
cards.pit: This is the silent assumption behind Kac's formula and behind every expected hitting time.

cards.q: Irreducible finite chain started at $i$, with $T = \min\{n \ge 1 : X_n = i\}$ and $\mathbb{E}(T) < \infty$. Let $r(j)$ be the expected number of visits to $j$ at the times $0, 1, \dots, T - 1$. (1) Give a formula for $r(j)$, the value $r(i)$ and the sum $\sum_j r(j)$. (2) Show $(\bar rP)(k) = r(k)$ for $k \ne i$. (3) Show it for $k = i$. (4) Conclude $\mathbb{E}(T) = 1/\pi(i)$.
pts: (1) $r(j) = \sum_{n \ge 0}\mathbb{P}\{X_n = j, T > n\}$; $r(i) = 1$ (only the visit at time 0); $\sum_j r(j) = \sum_{n \ge 0}\mathbb{P}\{T > n\} = \mathbb{E}(T)$.

(2) $\sum_j r(j)p(j, k) = \sum_{n \ge 0}\mathbb{P}\{X_{n+1} = k, T > n\}$ by the Markov property at time $n$. That is the expected number of visits to $k$ at the times $1, \dots, T$, which for $k \ne i$ equals $r(k)$: there is no visit to $k$ at time 0 or at time $T$.
(3) $\sum_{n \ge 0}\mathbb{P}\{X_{n+1} = i, T > n\} = \sum_{n \ge 0}\mathbb{P}\{T = n + 1\} = 1 = r(i)$.
(4) $\bar r$ is a nonnegative invariant vector with finite sum $\mathbb{E}(T)$, so by uniqueness $\bar r = \mathbb{E}(T)\bar\pi$. At $i$: $1 = \mathbb{E}(T)\pi(i)$.

cards.q: Random walk on a circle of $N$ points $\{0, \dots, N-1\}$, started at 0, each step to one of the two neighbours with probability $\tfrac12$. Show that the last point to be visited is uniformly distributed on $\{1, \dots, N-1\}$. (1) Characterise “$k$ is visited last”. (2) Reduce to a gambler's-ruin problem. (3) Compute the probability. (4) Conclude.
pts: (1) $k$ is last exactly when both neighbours of $k$ are visited before $k$.

(2) Stop at the first time the walk is at a neighbour of $k$ (possibly time 0). From there it must reach the other neighbour before $k$. Going the long way round, the other neighbour is $N - 2$ steps away, while $k$ is 1 step away in the other direction.
(3) Fair gambler's ruin on $\{0, \dots, N-1\}$ started at 1, with 0 = the point $k$ and $N - 1$ = the other neighbour: the probability of reaching $N - 1$ first is $\tfrac{1}{N-1}$.
(4) The value does not depend on which neighbour came first nor on $k$: each of the $N - 1$ points is last with probability $\tfrac{1}{N-1}$.
cards.pit: Surprising: the point next to the start is as likely to be last as the point opposite.

cards.q: A transition matrix $P$ is given. (1) What is done before any computing? (2) Which tool gives: the probability of a state at step $n$; the long-run fraction of time at $j$; $p_n(i, j)$ for large $n$? (3) Which tool gives: a mean return time; the mean number of steps from $j$ to $i \ne j$; the probability of reaching $A$ before $B$; the number of visits to a state before absorption? (4) Name four cross-checks.
pts: (1) Write the states and $P$ and check the row sums; draw the graph and find the communication classes (closed = recurrent, the rest transient); find the period of each recurrent class (self-loop gives 1; otherwise gcd of loop lengths, or bipartite).
(2) $\phi P^n$. Solve $\bar\pi P = \bar\pi$, $\sum\pi = 1$ (irreducible is enough; for a graph walk $d(v)/2e$). Aperiodic: $\pi(j)$; periodic: by cyclic group; reducible: $\alpha_k(i)\pi^k(j)$.
(3) Kac, $1/\pi(i)$. Make $i$ absorbing and take $M\bar 1$. Make $A$ and $B$ absorbing and take $MS$. The entry of $M$. Each can also be done with one-step equations.
(4) Rows of $P$ sum to 1; $\sum\pi = 1$; Kac agrees with one-step equations (e.g. $8 = 1 + 7$); each row of $MS$ sums to 1.

cards.q: (1) What is the difference between the invariant distribution $\bar\pi$ and the rows of $\lim_n P^n$, and when do they coincide? (2) Give a chain where $\bar\pi$ exists but $P^n$ does not converge. (3) Give one where $P^n$ converges but the rows differ. (4) Compare the two-state chains with $(p, q) = (\tfrac12, \tfrac13)$ and $(\tfrac14, \tfrac16)$, where $p = p(0, 1)$ and $q = p(1, 0)$.
pts: (1) $\bar\pi$ solves $\bar\pi P = \bar\pi$; the rows of $\lim P^n$ are the distribution after a long time, for each start. They coincide for irreducible aperiodic chains.
(2) The reflecting walk on $\{0, \dots, 4\}$: $\bar\pi = (\tfrac18, \tfrac14, \tfrac14, \tfrac14, \tfrac18)$ but $P^n$ alternates between even and odd $n$.
(3) The absorbing walk: row 1 tends to $(.75, 0, 0, 0, .25)$ and row 3 to $(.25, 0, 0, 0, .75)$.

(4) Both have $\bar\pi = (\tfrac25, \tfrac35)$ and mean return time $\tfrac52$ to state 0. The second eigenvalues are $\tfrac16$ and $\tfrac{7}{12}$: the first chain converges much faster. $\bar\pi$ fixes long-run fractions and mean return times, not the speed.

cards.q: (1) Classify the states of the chain on $\{0, 1, 2\}$ with $P = \begin{pmatrix}1/2&1/2&0\\0&1&0\\1/3&1/3&1/3\end{pmatrix}$. (2) Find $Q$ and $M$ in the order $0, 2$. (3) Find the expected number of steps to absorption from 0 and from 2. (4) Find $\lim_n P^n$. (5) Fair gambler's ruin with $N = 10$, starting from 3: the probability of reaching 10 and the expected number of rounds.
pts: (1) 1 is absorbing (recurrent class $\{1\}$); 0 and 2 are transient (0 reaches 1 and never comes back; 2 reaches 0 and 1).
(2) $Q = \begin{pmatrix}1/2&0\\1/3&1/3\end{pmatrix}$, $I - Q = \begin{pmatrix}1/2&0\\-1/3&2/3\end{pmatrix}$, $M = \begin{pmatrix}2&0\\1&3/2\end{pmatrix}$.
(3) Row sums: 2 from state 0, $\tfrac52$ from state 2.
(4) There is only one absorbing state, so every row tends to $(0, 1, 0)$.
